title: ABCDE Criteria for Melanoma Assessment
content: The ABCDE framework is used to evaluate pigmented lesions for melanoma risk: A = Asymmetry (one half does not match the other), B = Border irregularity (ragged, notched, or blurred edges), C = Color variation (shades of brown, black, pink, red, white, or blue within the same lesion), D = Diameter (greater than 6mm, though melanomas can be smaller), E = Evolving (change in size, shape, color, or symptoms like itching, bleeding, or elevation over time).

title: Fitzpatrick Phototype Classification
content: Fitzpatrick skin phototypes classify skin according to its response to UV radiation: Type I: Always burns, never tans (very fair, red hair, freckles). Type II: Usually burns, tans minimally (fair, light hair). Type III: Sometimes mild burn, uniform tan (medium skin tone). Type IV: Burns minimally, tans easily (olive skin). Type V: Seldom burns, tans profusely (dark brown skin). Type VI: Never burns, deeply pigmented (black skin).

title: Atopic Dermatitis (Eczema) Clinical Features & Management
content: Atopic dermatitis manifests as pruritic, erythematous, ill-defined papules and plaques with scaling, lichenification, and occasional excoriation. Frequently affects flexural surfaces (antecubital and popliteal fossae) in adults and facial/extensor surfaces in infants. Primary management includes gentle soap-free cleansers, barrier repair emollients (ceramides, petrolatum), topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors, and avoiding known environmental triggers.

title: Plaque Psoriasis Clinical Presentation
content: Plaque psoriasis is characterized by sharply demarcated, erythematous plaques covered with silvery-white scales. Common anatomical sites include extensor surfaces (elbows, knees), scalp, lumbosacral region, and nails (pitting, oil drop sign, onycholysis). Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding upon scale removal) and Koebner phenomenon (lesions developing at sites of skin trauma) are classic diagnostic indicators.

title: Acne Vulgaris Pathophysiology & Evidence-Based Treatment
content: Acne vulgaris stems from hyperkeratinization, excess sebum production driven by androgenic stimulation, Cutibacterium acnes colonization, and perifollicular inflammation. Non-inflammatory lesions include open (blackheads) and closed (whiteheads) comedones. Inflammatory lesions include papules, pustules, nodules, and cysts. First-line treatments combine topical retinoids (adapalene, tretinoin) with benzoyl peroxide and/or topical antibiotics.

title: Rosacea Subtypes & Clinical Characteristics
content: Rosacea primarily affects central facial areas (cheeks, nose, forehead, chin). Subtypes include: 1) Erythematotelangiectatic: Persistent facial erythema and flushing with fine telangiectasias. 2) Papulopustular: Central facial erythema with transient papules and pustules (lacks comedones, distinguishing it from acne). 3) Phymatous: Tissue hypertrophy (e.g. rhinophyma). 4) Ocular: Blepharitis, conjunctival hyperemia, stye formation.

title: Tinea Corporis (Ringworm) Clinical Diagnostic Features
content: Tinea corporis presents as an annular, erythematous plaque with a raised scaly advancing border and central clearing. Caused by dermatophytes (Trichophyton rubrum, Microsporum, Epidermophyton). Potassium hydroxide (KOH) wet mount examination reveals segmented branching hyphae. Topical azoles (clotrimazole, miconazole, terbinafine) are first-line unless extensive or refractory.

title: Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) Morphology
content: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer. Nodular BCC presents as a pearly, translucent papule or nodule with telangiectasias, rolled borders, and central ulceration (rodent ulcer). Superficial BCC appears as a erythematous scaly patch resembling eczema or psoriasis. Usually develops on sun-exposed skin (head, neck, back). Treatment includes surgical excision, Mohs surgery, or electrodesiccation.

title: Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) Risk & Features
content: Squamous cell carcinoma often arises from precursor actinic keratoses on sun-damaged skin. Presents as a firm, erythematous hyperkeratotic papule, nodule, or non-healing ulcer with cutaneous horn formation. Higher metastatic risk compared to BCC, particularly on lip, ear, or immunosuppressed patients. Histopathology shows keratin pearls and atypical keratinocytes.

title: Allergic vs Irritant Contact Dermatitis
content: Contact dermatitis manifests as localized pruritic erythema, edema, and vesiculation. Irritant contact dermatitis results from direct cytotoxic chemical exposure (soaps, solvents) and occurs immediately upon exposure. Allergic contact dermatitis is a Type IV delayed hypersensitivity response (poison ivy/urushiol, nickel, fragrances, neomycin) requiring prior sensitization and presenting 24-72 hours after exposure.
